newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany turns austerity on civil servants pensions.
newsitem.headline: Germany turns austerity on civil servants pensions.

text.p: Interior Minister Manfred Kanther said on Friday Germany must now rein in the cost of civil servants' pensions after giving private sector employers more freedom to curb personnel costs.
The increase in such costs is outpacing economic growth, a situation Kanther termed intolerable and said austerity measures are overdue.
Kanther said if nothing is done, pension costs for civil servants will double by the year 2008, and the problem will become acute between 2015 and 2030.
The OeTV civil servants' union and the Beamtenbund federation immediately disputed Kanther's analysis and his proposals.

Opposition Social Democratic (SPD) leader Oskar Lafontaine, in an interview with the Handelsblatt newspaper, joined Kanther in warning that civil servants' pension costs could escalate out of control.
Lafontaine said the civil servants' privileged status was unjust, and accused the government of proceeding too cautiously. "What the government has done so far is not worthy of the name reform."
The main reason for the ballooning costs is the large number of teachers, police officers and court employees hired in the 1960s and 1970s, who will reach retirement age in coming decades.
Under Germany's social umbrella, the state funds pensions for most civil servants, who have lifetime tenure. In exchange for those privileges, the employees give up the right to strike.
With conservative estimates of annual increases of 1.5 to 3.0 percent, civil servants' pensions would rise to 69 billion marks in 2008 and 120 billion marks in 2020 from 34.1 billion marks in 1993.

Kanther proposed that lifetime civil servants forfeit a portion of their wage increases starting in the year 2000, to fund part of the pension burden. Withholding even 0.2 percent a year could mean savings of 60 billion marks.
